Vṛśa Jāna (‘descendant of Jana’) is the name of a famous purohita, who was unfortunate enough, while with his royal master, Tryaruṇa, to see a boy killed by the chariot which the king drove too fast. He thereupon recalled the boy to life. The story is told briefly in the pañcaviṃśa brāhmaṇa, the Śāṭyāyanaka, the Tāṇḍaka, was also narrated in the bhāllavi brāhmaṇa, and is preserved in the Bṛhaddevatā, Sieg has endeavoured to trace the story in part in the Rigveda, but there is a consensus of opinion against the correctness of such a view.

Vṛścika in the Rigveda and the Atharvaveda denote ‘scorpion.’ Its poison was feared like that of serpents. It is described as lying torpid in the earth during winter.

Vṛṣa is the name of a plant of some kind in the kāṭhaka Saṃhitā. Later the Gendarussa vulgaris is so styled. Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā has Vṛśa, which Bo7htlingk takes to mean a small animal, a quite possible sense. Cf. yevāṣa.

Vṛṣa-khādi is used as an epithet of the Maruts in the Rigveda. The sense is doubtful: Bollensen thought the expression referred to the wearing of rings in the ears; Max Müller renders it ‘strong rings,’ comparing the later cakra or discus.

Vṛṣa-gaṇa is the name of a family of singers mentioned in one passage of the Rigveda.
Foot notes ix. 97, 8. Cf. Ludwig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 132.

Vṛṣaṇ-aśva is the name of a man referred to in the Rigveda, where indra is called menā, perhaps his ‘wife’ or ‘daughter.’ The same legend is alluded to in the Jaiminīya brāhmaṇa, the Śatapatha brāhmaṇa, the Ṣaḍviṃśa brāhmaṇa, and the taittirīya Āraṇyaka, but it is clear that all of these texts had no real tradition of what was referred to.

Vṛṣa-daṃśa, ‘strong-toothed,’ is the name of the cat in the yajurveda Saṃhitās, where it figures as a victim at the aśvamedha (‘horse sacrifice’). It also appears in the pañcaviṃśa brāhmaṇa; the fact that the sneeze of the cat is here referred to renders it likely that the animal was already tamed. Geldner sees a house cat in the animal alluded to in a hymn of the Atharvaveda by a set of curious epithets, including vṛṣadatī, ‘strong-toothed,’ but Whitney decisively rejects the idea that the hymn refers to the domestic cat.
Foot notes taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 5, 21, 1; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 14, 12; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 31.

Vṛṣan in two passages of the Rigveda seems to denote a man, with the patronymic pāthya in one of them.
Foot notes i. 36, 10; vi. 16, 14. 15. Cf. Max Müller, Sacred Books of the East, 32, 152, 153; Ludwig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 104.

Vṛṣabha regularly denotes a ‘bull’ in the Rigveda, but usually in a metaphorical sense.
Foot notes i. 94, 10; 160, 3; vi. 46, 4; of Parjanya, vii. 101, 1, 6, etc. Roth renders vrsabhānna, ii. 16, 5, ‘eating strong food’; but the literal sense, ‘whose food is bulls,’ will answer. Cf. māṃsa.

Vṛṣala in the dicing hymn of the Rigveda denotes an ‘outcast’; the same sense appears in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka upaniṣad, where the touch of either a vṛṣala or a Vṛṣalī is to be avoided.
Foot notes x. 34, 11. Cf. nirukta, iii. 16.

Vṛṣa-śuṣma Vātāvata (‘descendant of Vātāvant’) jātūkarṇya is the name of a priest in the Brāhmaṇas of the Rigveda. Vṛṣaśuṣma in the vaṃśa brāhmaṇa is probably intended for the same name.
Foot notes aitareya brāhmaṇa, v. 29, 1; kauṣītaki brāhmaṇa, ii. 9 (with a varia lectio vādhāvata: Indische Studien, 1, 215, n. 1).
Indische Studien, 4, 373.

Vṛṣā-rava, ‘roaring like a bull,’ is the name of some animal in the Rigveda. In the Śatapatha brāhmaṇa the word occurs in the dual, meaning perhaps ‘mallet’ or ‘drumstick.’
Foot notes x. 146, 2 = taittirīya brāhmaṇa, ii. 5, 5, 6.

Vṛṣṭi is the regular word for ‘rain’ in the Rigveda and later.

Vṛṣṭi-havya is in the Rigveda the name of a ṛṣi, whose sons were the Upastutas.
Foot notes x. 115, 9. Cf. Max Mūller, Sacred Books of the East, 32, 152, 153; Ludwig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 108, 109.
